lesson.title: Where You Start Determines How You Get There
lesson.summary: Real RC and RL circuits rarely begin from zero, so finding the correct starting point, using the fact that capacitor voltage and inductor current cannot change instantly, is essential before the exponential response can be written down.
lesson.body:
The RC and RL circuit examples worked so far both conveniently started from zero: an uncharged capacitor, a de-energized inductor. Real circuits are rarely so tidy. A capacitor may already be sitting at some charged voltage from an earlier part of its history, or an inductor may already be carrying current, before whatever change (a switch closing, a source stepping to a new value) is even applied. Handling that properly, without changing the underlying shape or time constant of the exponential response, is what initial conditions covers.

Two physical continuity rules make this possible. Capacitor voltage cannot change instantaneously, written Vc(0 minus) = Vc(0 plus), because an instant jump in voltage would require moving a finite amount of charge onto the plates in zero time, which means infinite current, which is not physically possible. Inductor current cannot change instantaneously, written I(0 minus) = I(0 plus), for the mirror image reason: an instant jump in current would require infinite voltage, since voltage across an inductor is proportional to how fast current is changing. Everything else in a circuit, resistor voltages, resistor currents, capacitor current, inductor voltage, is free to jump instantly. Only capacitor voltage and inductor current are protected by continuity.

The general method follows directly from that fact: find the relevant value just before the change, at time 0 minus, usually the steady state of whatever circuit existed beforehand. Carry that value across the switching instant unchanged, as the initial condition at 0 plus. Then find the new steady state, the final value the circuit is heading toward as time goes to infinity in its new configuration. Finally, connect those two values with an exponential curve, using whatever time constant applies to the new circuit.

Worked example: a capacitor with C = 50 microfarads has been sitting in an earlier circuit long enough to settle at a steady 10 volts. At t = 0, a switch reconfigures the circuit so the capacitor now discharges through a fresh resistor R = 5 kilohms, with no source connected at all. Continuity gives Vc(0 plus) = 10 volts, the value carries over unchanged rather than resetting to zero. The new time constant is tau = RC = 5000 times 0.00005 = 0.25 seconds. The final value, as t goes to infinity with no source, is 0 volts. So the full response is Vc(t) = 10 times e to the power of negative t over 0.25. After exactly one time constant, t = 0.25 seconds, Vc = 10 times e to the negative 1 = 10 times 0.3679, about 3.68 volts.

This find the initial value, find the final value, find tau, then connect them with an exponential method works for any circuit containing a single capacitor or single inductor, no matter how complicated the surrounding resistor network looks. It is also exactly the setup needed for the next step up in complexity, the RLC circuit, where a capacitor and inductor's two separate continuity rules must be tracked at the same time.
